title: Why AI Cannot Write Emotional Scenes: Objective Projection as a Framework for Auditable Narrative Generation
abstract: Large language models consistently produce emotionally labeled prose when prompted to generate affective narrative content. This paper argues that the failure is not technical but architectural: current AI systems optimize for statistical pattern reproduction, reproducing the most frequent emotional label constructions in their training corpora rather than encoding the physical conditions that produce physiological responses in readers. We introduce Objective Projection (Nesnel İzdüşüm), a narrative engineering methodology that replaces emotional labels with measurable physical parameters derived from the Autonomic Activation Window (AAW) of target physiological states. The methodology's central claim — that physical parameter specification produces more consistent, more cross-culturally stable, and more auditable narrative output than emotional label specification — is formalized through the concept of Narrative Entropy (Sₙ = ∫(If × Cb) dt), where Information Friction (If) and Causal Branching (Cb) function as measurable proxies for reader engagement. We document the Output Layer principle, which specifies that physical parameters govern narrative generation without appearing in the generated text, and present the Objective Projection Calibration Test (OPCT v2.0, pre-registered OSF: osf.io/us8bw) as an empirical validation framework. The paper concludes that Objective Projection offers the digital humanities a reproducible, parameter-based approach to narrative generation that is amenable to systematic evaluation and independent replication. Keywords: narrative engineering, large language models, emotional generation, physical parameters, Objective Projection, Narrative Entropy, digital humanities, prompt engineering, computational narratology Official: https://leventbulut.com/

title: Distributed Federated Learning with Differential Privacy for Collaborative Graph Analytics
abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training machine learning models on decentralized data sources without directly exchanging the raw data. However, the application of FL to graph analytics, particularly when dealing with sensitive graph data, presents significant challenges due to the inherent privacy risks associated with sharing graph structures and node attributes. This paper proposes a novel distributed federated learning framework incorporating differential privacy (DP) to address these challenges. The framework leverages secure aggregation techniques to minimize information leakage during model aggregation and integrates local differential privacy mechanisms at the node level to provide robust privacy guarantees. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and conceptual design, highlighting its potential to enable collaborative graph analytics while preserving the privacy of participating nodes. The key contributions of this work include a tailored FL architecture for graph data, the integration of DP for enhanced privacy, and a discussion of the trade-offs involved in balancing privacy and model accuracy.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Optimization through Adaptive Resonance Networks
abstract: Quantum-enhanced optimization through Adaptive Resonance Networks (QORANs) presents a novel approach to solving complex optimization problems by integrating the principles of quantum computing with the adaptive resonance network (ARN) framework. This paper explores the potential of QORANs to accelerate convergence and improve the search process in areas such as machine learning, combinatorial optimization, and financial modeling. We detail the methodology, theoretical underpinnings, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach. The core claim is that combining quantum computation with ARNs leads to a significantly enhanced optimization algorithm with improved search capabilities.

title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks with Bayesian Dropout and Adaptive Learning Rates
abstract: This paper addresses the inherent vulnerability of neural networks to noisy training data and outliers, a critical limitation impacting their generalization performance. We propose a novel self-correcting neural network architecture designed to mitigate these issues. The architecture integrates Bayesian dropout, an adaptive learning rate scheme, and an outlier detection and mitigation strategy. Bayesian dropout introduces stochasticity during training, effectively creating an ensemble of subnetworks and reducing overfitting. Adaptive learning rates dynamically adjust the learning rate for each parameter based on its historical gradients, accelerating convergence and improving robustness. Furthermore, a dedicated outlier detection module identifies and downweights the influence of anomalous training samples. This comprehensive approach results in a neural network that is significantly more resilient to noise and outliers, leading to improved accuracy and stability during training and deployment. The theoretical framework presented provides a foundation for understanding the combined effect of these components, and the architecture demonstrates promising results across a range of benchmark datasets.

title: Dynamic Quantum Potential Computing Model
abstract: This paper presents a novel computational model based on dynamic quantum potential fields, designed to efficiently model and solve complex systems by dynamically adjusting quantum potential landscapes. Traditional computational methods often struggle with intricate equations and complex system behavior. This model leverages the unique properties of quantum computers to achieve high-precision calculations across a range of applications. The core mechanism involves a sophisticated system of quantum potential fields that are continuously updated and refined, enabling the simulation of dynamic systems and the resolution of challenging equations. This approach overcomes limitations of static models, offering a promising path toward improved computational power and accuracy in modeling complex phenomena.

title: Certified Panic Mode: the recovery-quality campaign archive
abstract: The data behind the evaluation section of Certified Panic Mode: Repair-Invariant Error Recovery for Maximal-Munch Lexing. It is deposited on its own so that the archive has an identifier independent of the manuscript and of the library the manuscript measures. What is here. The root of the archive is the campaign archive as the manuscript describes it: the paper's own tree keeps those files under data/, and they sit at the root here. Its README.md documents what it holds: the recovery-quality campaign runs, the revision-six run among them carrying a per-move sidecar, the probe summaries, the five generated corpora, the analysis programs that derive the manuscript's figures from the archives, and the pinned reproduction scripts. The real document is not here; see below. checker/ holds an independent from-scratch reference model of maximal-munch scanning, reference.py, and witnesses.py, nine author-selected bounded semantic checks executed against it; which of them the manuscript still states, and whether they cover it, is the author's mapping and is not machine-checked. These do not read the campaign archive. They check semantics the programs can execute against a model written separately from the library, which is a different question from whether the campaign reproduces, and they are deposited beside it because a reader who wants one usually wants the other. Verifying it. Two ledgers, each covering its own part, both self-contained here: run sha256sum -c manifest.txt at the root for the campaign archive, and sha256sum -c MANIFEST.txt inside checker/ for the reference model, each naming entries relative to the directory it is run from. Between them those two cover every file here except three that are about the archive rather than part of it: DEPOSIT.md and the two ledgers themselves. The checker's own ignore file stays in the repository and is not deposited. To reproduce the campaign itself rather than check its bytes, reproduce-r6.sh is the pinned script; it checks out the library's v1.6.0 release, archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22544477, and verifies the harness it builds against the snapshot archived here. The manuscript's own gate runs the analysis programs and compares their output with the committed emissions. Three of the derived files are read directly by the manuscript: the pooled table, the landing figure's table, and the overhang data file, so no plotted-series coordinate is transcribed between this archive and the document; the figure's two hand-placed annotations are checked by eye. The statistics text, the mechanism text, and the landing CSV are archived companion outputs rather than direct manuscript inputs. The real document. The real-document row runs on twitter.json, the simdjson benchmark corpus, 631,515 bytes, byte-identical to jsonexamples/twitter.json at that project's release v3.10.1. It is not redistributed here. It is third-party content, real social media posts, and this archive carries no rights in it, so the reproduction scripts fetch it from that pinned release and hold it to the SHA-256 recorded beside them in corpus.sha256, 30721e49... That is the same guarantee a bundled copy gave, and those scripts already clone the library, so fetching it adds no new network requirement, though it does require curl. No analysis program in this archive reads the corpus. Everything in this deposit is the author's own work and is released under CC BY 4.0.

title: Companion-style QA Assistance in Ego-Vision
abstract: AI companions are envisioned as always-on assistants that support users in daily life. With this regard, we introduce BuddyVQA, a benchmark for companion-style question answering (QA) on egocentric streaming video. BuddyVQA contains 21.6K questions linked to 6K highlight moments across 1,012 long, egocentric videos. It features two key characteristics that are common in daily first-person QA assistance but are largely overlooked in existing VideoQA benchmarks: ego-deictic expressions and interactively chained questions (e.g., "Where is it?", "How to get there?"). These require models to infer a user's in-situation intent by resolving visual pronouns in the context of egocentric visual and QA contents, with both grounded in a long-form streaming setting. To tackle the challenges, we propose MyBuddy, a companion-style QA assistant that highlights a multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism to infer the final answer based on the historical QA and visual content. An additional question filter and multi-level memory are designed to facilitate efficient QA and visual information retrieval under streaming QA settings. Experiments show that MyBuddy significantly enhances the performance of foundation models on BuddyVQA. Moreover, these gains generalize to other streaming and common video QA benchmarks, demonstrating the applicability and effectiveness of our approach. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/QHUni/BuddyVQA

Experiments show that MyBuddy significantly enhances the performance of foundation models on BuddyVQA. Moreover, these gains generalize to other streaming and common video QA benchmarks, demonstrating the applicability and effectiveness of our approach. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/QHUni/BuddyVQA

title: Unifying Physics-Based Humanoid Interaction with a Context-Conditioned Interaction Prior
abstract: Developing unified physics-based humanoid controllers that can navigate complex 3D scenes and manipulate objects remains a longstanding challenge. Existing approaches are often specialized for either locomotion or object-centric manipulation, or rely on task-specific reward engineering that does not scale well across diverse behaviors. We present CHIP, a unified, physics-grounded framework for learning reusable humanoid interaction skills from heterogeneous motion data. Central to our approach is a conditional interaction prior that models a context-dependent distribution over these skills within a shared discrete space. Our method is trained in three stages. We first learn physics-based motion-imitation policies that acquire grounded teacher behaviors from heterogeneous interaction data. We then distill these behaviors into a context-conditioned interaction prior that captures reusable motion structure across locomotion and manipulation. Finally, we initialize downstream task policies from the pretrained prior and adapt them through prior-regularized online RL post-training. Experiments on a diverse suite of humanoid interaction tasks show that our approach supports scene-aware locomotion, contact-rich object manipulation, and compositional behaviors such as environment-aware object transport and long-horizon skill sequencing, while producing smooth transitions and physically plausible motion.

title: A Controlled Single-Thread Benchmark of PennyLane, Qiskit, and Snowflurry for Ideal Statevector Circuit Simulation
abstract: This study presents a reproducible, framework-level comparison of three open-source quantum software environments: PennyLane 0.45.1, Qiskit 2.5.2, and Snowflurry 0.6.0. Equivalent parameterized circuits were constructed in Python for PennyLane and Qiskit and in Julia for Snowflurry. Every circuit consisted of repeated layers of single-qubit rotations followed by a ring of controlled-NOT gates, and every framework returned the complete ideal statevector. Circuit construction time, first-execution time, warmed execution time, whole-process wall time, output probability, and state normalization were recorded. All common numerical thread controls were fixed to one, so the experiment measures controlled single-thread behavior rather than the maximum throughput of the tested computers. On the laptop, Snowflurry produced the lowest warmed median at 10 qubits, Qiskit at 12 qubits, PennyLane and Qiskit were nearly tied at 14 qubits, and PennyLane was fastest at 18 qubits. On an Intel Xeon E5-2697 v3 workstation, PennyLane was fastest at both 14 and 16 qubits. Snowflurry constructed circuits rapidly but exhibited greater simulation time as the statevector increased. Identical probabilities and unit state norms across all implementations support functional equivalence. The results characterize these particular built-in statevector paths; they do not constitute a general comparison of Python and Julia, nor of optimized accelerators such as PennyLane Lightning or Qiskit Aer.

title: The Invariant Science: A Formal Calculus of Legitimate Transformation with P-Full Completion as a P versus NP Case
abstract: This paper proposes Invariant Science as a formal research program for studying what must remain preserved, what may transform lawfully, and what may survive only up to an explicitly declared equivalence when a scientific object moves across representations, models, scales, decompositions, observers, environments, or time. The proposal is motivated by a recurrent methodological difficulty: scientific progress often depends on transformations, yet the legitimacy of a transformed claim is rarely represented as a first-class mathematical object. We introduce the Algebra of Legitimate Scientific Transformation (ALST) as the general theory and the Invariant Trajectory Calculus (ITC) as a typed calculus of states, invariants, certificates, transformations, semantic reconstruction, composition, resource bounds, abolition, residual strengthening, and terminal admission. The central object is a legitimate trajectory rather than a privileged representation. A transformation earns scientific status only when the mission-relevant identity can be reconstructed, the required certificates are checkable, and the declared resource obligations remain inside their contract. We distinguish exact, equivariant, quotient, and obstruction invariants; separate the object-derivation plane from the research-revision plane; formalize Original-Scale Polynomial Closure so that a sequence of locally polynomial steps cannot hide superpolynomial growth; and state soundness results for composition, polynomial strong normalization, and certified progress. P-Full Completion is then introduced as Case 001. A P-full terminal regime is a uniformly recognizable and polynomially decidable regime equipped with the reconstruction machinery needed to recover the original decision. Weak P-Full Completion is shown to collapse to ordinary polynomial-time decidability when arbitrary terminal regimes are permitted, motivating Structural P-Full Completion, in which the rule basis, terminal families, applicability tests, and resource signatures are fixed independently of the input answer. For a fixed NP-complete language, a uniform Structural P-Full Completion system satisfying the stated soundness and global-cost conditions would imply P = NP. This is not claimed here. The contribution is instead a falsifiable mathematical architecture that isolates the exact residual obligations such a transformation-based proof would have to discharge, especially universal P-full sink coverage or an equivalent certified progress theorem. The paper positions these objects relative to complexity theory, tractable constraint languages, backdoors, SAT preprocessing, proof complexity, knowledge compilation, parameterized complexity, and term rewriting, and concludes with a research program designed to allow both constructive and impossibility results.

title: IronClad AI Agent Research Series: Context Engineering, Multi-Tiered Memory, and Mathematical Foundations for Autonomous Local LLM Systems
abstract: This Zenodo archive deposits the foundational research white paper series for the **IronClad AI Agent**, a Rust-native autonomous agent orchestration runtime engineered specifically for local Large Language Models (LLMs) executing under strict consumer hardware constraints (8–24 GB VRAM, finite 8K–32K context windows, and bounded memory bandwidth). Traditional autonomous agent architectures rely heavily on qualitative prompts and heuristics ("prompt-and-pray") suited for unconstrained cloud APIs with >100B parameter models. When deployed locally on quantized open-weight models (7B–27B, such as DeepSeek-R1, QwQ, and Qwen 2.5), these systems suffer from severe failure modes: Key-Value cache memory exhaustion, attention degradation ("Lost in the Middle"), runaway token dissipation on trivial queries, tool repetition loops, and non-deterministic security bypasses. This deposit comprises two complementary research papers that provide both the **empirical systems architecture** and the **underlying mathematical formalization** to solve these challenges deterministically: --- ## Part I: Context Engineering and Multi-Tiered Memory Architectures for Local Large Language Model Agents: Mitigating Token Bloat, Context Degradation, and Trivial Task Overthinking * **Document:** `white_paper_context_memory.pdf` * **Focus:** Empirical systems architecture, memory isolation, and reasoning token hygiene. * **Core Contributions:** 1. **Four-Tier Memory Architecture:** Cleanly decouples Working Memory (scratchpads/checkpoints), Core Fact Key-Value Storage, Episodic Session Learnings, and Tree-sitter AST Graph RAG to eliminate global prompt injection. 2. **Intent Fast-Bypass Classifier:** Short-circuits compute-heavy reasoning cycles (` ... `) on simple conversational queries (e.g., greetings, status lookups), preventing 1,000+ token reasoning waste on trivial inputs. 3. **File-Backed Telemetry Offloading:** Caps in-context tool payloads (compiler logs, test traces, diffs) at 8,000 characters with head/tail sampling while persisting raw telemetry to disk. 4. **Recursive Summarization Pipeline:** Dynamically compresses historical dialogue turns before sliding-window eviction to preserve multi-session coherence. 5. **Archetype-Aware Dynamic Model Routing (ADR-006):** Matches task complexity dynamically to available quantized local models. * **Empirical Validation:** Demonstrates up to **78.4% prompt token overhead reduction**, **91.2% lower latency** on conversational turns, **100% token reasoning hygiene**, and **90.0% multi-turn autonomous completion** on local hardware. --- ## Part II: Mathematical Foundations of Autonomous Local Agent Systems: Formalizing Model Routing, Tree Search Rewards, Vector Gating, Temporal Decay, and Security Lattices in IronClad AI Agent * **Document:** `white_paper_mathematical_foundations.pdf` * **Focus:** Rigorous mathematical formulations, proofs of efficacy, and failure boundary analysis. * **Core Formulations:** 1. **Dynamic Task Archetype Scoring & Model Routing ($S_{\text{Archetype}}$):** Formulates model selection via high-dimensional weighted linear projections across an 8-Pillar capability space ($\mathbf{P} \in [0, 1]^8$). 2. **Process Reward Models (PRM) & Step-Level Verification:** Defines objective, non-heuristic per-step reward functions $R(s_t, a_t)$ with verifiable termination conditions. 3. **Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with Budget Constraints:** Establishes Upper Confidence bounds for Trees (UCT) adapted for non-stationary local agent branching and bounded rollout depth. 4. **AST Semantic Graph RAG:** Proves context allocation bounds and cosine similarity gating inequalities for semantic syntax-tree chunking. 5. **Temporal Memory Confidence Decay:** Models episodic memory reliability via geometric half-life dissipation curves over time. 6. **Governor Security Lattices:** Formalizes access control and dangerous tool execution via supremum operators over totally ordered risk partially ordered sets (posets). 7. **IronClad Composite Intelligence Index (ICII):** Standardized, multidimensional benchmark metric for local agentic autonomy. 8. **Critical Theoretical Audit:** Formulates explicit assumptions, convergence proofs, and failure boundary conditions (degenerate distributions, sparsity breakdowns, and context edge cases). ---

title: Modular Quantum Field Theory – Emergent Scale Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for constructing quantum field theories – Modular Quantum Field Theory (MQTF) – based on the design and assembly of reusable quantum components. We propose a method for generating complex field states by combining pre-defined modules, facilitating rapid exploration of theoretical phenomena. The core mechanism centers around creating a system of quantum components that can be dynamically assembled, allowing for effortless exploration of diverse scenarios and emergent behavior. The paper details the design of a modular system, outlining the core principles of component construction and the potential for creating complex quantum states through their interactions. We discuss the advantages of this approach in terms of scalability, adaptability, and the potential for uncovering novel quantum phenomena.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: A Self-Adaptive Gradient Descent Algorithm
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning has emerged as a promising field, offering the potential to accelerate machine learning algorithms and enhance their capabilities. This paper introduces a novel quantum machine learning algorithm, termed "Self-Adaptive Gradient Descent," that leverages the principles of quantum mechanics to dynamically adjust gradient descent parameters, enabling more efficient and accurate learning of complex neural networks. The core mechanism involves a quantum-enhanced gradient descent process, optimizing the parameters based on the data's inherent dynamics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through a series of experiments on a benchmark dataset, showcasing improved accuracy and faster convergence compared to traditional gradient descent methods. The core claim is that this algorithm can effectively learn complex neural networks and achieve more precise predictions.

title: Vector Field-Based Emergent Algorithm for Optimal Data Compression
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm, the Vector Field-Based Emergent Algorithm (VFBA), designed for optimal data compression. Traditional compression methods often rely on fixed parameters and struggle to adapt to complex data structures. The VFBA leverages vector field dynamics to create a dynamically updating representation of the data, achieving superior compression ratios and self-sustaining optimization. We detail the core mechanism, explain the underlying mathematics, and present preliminary results demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness. The research explores the potential of this approach to overcome the limitations of existing compression techniques.

title: Quantum State Encryption
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum state encryption, leveraging the inherent fragility of quantum states to develop a novel cryptographic protocol. The core claim centers on utilizing quantum state vulnerabilities to establish secure communication channels. We detail a proposed framework incorporating quantum state manipulation, specifically employing quantum state error correction to mitigate the risks associated with measurement and decoherence. The paper analyzes the theoretical and practical implications of this approach, highlighting potential advancements and challenges in the field. The focus is on the fundamental principles and potential benefits of this new encryption method, aiming to advance the state of quantum cryptography.

title: 基于自适应的概率空间建模
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to probabilistic modeling, termed "Adaptive Probability Space Modeling," designed to enhance prediction accuracy and robustness. Traditional modeling methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their ability to effectively capture the inherent complexities within the system being modeled. This work introduces a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism within a probabilistic space, allowing the model to adapt to the data and improve predictive performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through extensive simulations and experimental validation across diverse datasets. The core of this method lies in exploiting the inherent variability within the probability space itself, leading to more informed and reliable predictions. The resulting model exhibits improved generalization capabilities and resilience to noise and outliers.

title: Quantum Topology Geometry Optimization and Computation
abstract: Quantum topology geometry optimization is a novel approach to tackling complex optimization problems through the application of quantum algorithms. This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum computational techniques to transform traditional optimization challenges into a quantum-enhanced framework. We investigate the core mechanism, outlining the fundamental steps involved in leveraging quantum properties for improved geometric optimization. The research focuses on the advantages of quantum computation over classical methods, particularly in addressing intricate geometric constraints and exploring novel solution spaces. This work presents a detailed analysis of the algorithm's architecture, outlining the key quantum operations and their impact on the optimization process. The potential for significant computational speedup and the ability to tackle previously intractable problems are highlighted as key benefits of this approach. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and the anticipated impact on various fields, including materials science and engineering.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization for Complex Network Design
abstract: Quantum-inspired optimization provides a novel approach to designing complex networks, leveraging quantum mechanics to guide the exploration of potential architectures. This paper introduces a framework for utilizing quantum annealing to identify optimal network configurations, addressing the limitations of traditional optimization methods. The core claim is that integrating quantum-inspired techniques into network design can lead to enhanced performance and creative solutions. This work explores the application of quantum annealing to optimize network structures, demonstrating the potential for improved efficiency and design space exploration. The paper details the methodology, results, and implications of this research, emphasizing the advantages offered by quantum-inspired optimization in complex network design.

title: Title: Adaptive Information Bottleneck for Quantum Data Compression
abstract: Quantum data compression presents a significant challenge due to the inherent fragility of quantum states and the difficulty in representing them efficiently. Traditional methods often struggle with the exponential growth of state space, requiring substantial computational resources. This paper proposes an Adaptive Information Bottleneck (AIB) technique for quantum data compression, leveraging the information bottleneck principle to achieve efficient compression while safeguarding essential quantum information. The AIB framework dynamically adjusts the bottleneck size based on the state's characteristics, optimizing compression ratios and minimizing information loss. We present a novel implementation of the bottleneck-based compression algorithm, demonstrating its efficacy through simulations and initial experimental results on a small-scale quantum state. The paper explores the potential of AIB to address the limitations of existing quantum data compression methods and opens avenues for further research into quantum information processing.

title: Title: Hierarchical Bayesian Networks for Data Distribution Learning
abstract: Hierarchical Bayesian Networks (HBNs) offer a powerful framework for learning probabilistic models of data distribution by explicitly representing the network structure and learning a representation of the data at each level of abstraction. This paper introduces a novel hierarchical Bayesian Network architecture that automatically refines the network structure based on observed data, leading to improved distribution estimates and a more robust representation. We present a new method for constructing and learning HBNs that leverages a hierarchical structure to capture complex data dependencies. The core mechanism focuses on a dynamic network refinement process that adapts to the data, enhancing the model's ability to generalize. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through extensive experiments on a dataset of synthetic data, showcasing improved accuracy and robustness compared to existing methods. The results highlight the advantages of the proposed hierarchical Bayesian Network in data distribution learning.

title: Probabilistic Relational Logic for Dynamic Knowledge Graphs
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to representing and reasoning with dynamic knowledge graphs (KGs) using Probabilistic Relational Logic (PRL). Traditional methods for KG representation often struggle to effectively handle uncertainty and incomplete information, prevalent characteristics of real-world knowledge. PRL extends the foundational principles of relational logic by incorporating probability distributions to quantify the confidence associated with relationships between entities within a KG. This allows for the representation of vague or uncertain connections, enabling more robust and accurate inference. The core claim is that PRL provides a more expressive and robust representation capable of addressing the ambiguities inherent in real-world data. We outline the key components of PRL, including the formalism for defining probabilistic relations and reasoning techniques. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications and highlight the advantages of this approach compared to existing KG representation methods. The presented framework offers a significant step forward in building intelligent systems that can effectively manage and utilize dynamic knowledge graphs with inherent uncertainty.

PRL extends the foundational principles of relational logic by incorporating probability distributions to quantify the confidence associated with relationships between entities within a KG. This allows for the representation of vague or uncertain connections, enabling more robust and accurate inference. The core claim is that PRL provides a more expressive and robust representation capable of addressing the ambiguities inherent in real-world data. We outline the key components of PRL, including the formalism for defining probabilistic relations and reasoning techniques. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications and highlight the advantages of this approach compared to existing KG representation methods. The presented framework offers a significant step forward in building intelligent systems that can effectively manage and utilize dynamic knowledge graphs with inherent uncertainty.

title: 基于概率模型的高效算法设计
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to algorithm design centered around the construction of probabilistic models. The core idea is to model the behavior of an algorithm – specifically its runtime and resource consumption – using probability distributions. This allows for the application of optimization techniques, traditionally used in fields like engineering and operations research, to refine and improve the algorithm's performance. Unlike traditional heuristic or random search methods, this approach provides a quantifiable framework for algorithm design, leading to potentially more efficient and predictable results. The key lies in leveraging the statistical properties of the algorithm's execution to guide optimization, ultimately aiming for algorithms with superior performance characteristics. This work outlines the theoretical foundations and presents a methodology for designing efficient algorithms through probabilistic modeling and optimization.

title: Algorithmic Quantum Resonance Mapping
abstract: This paper explores the concept of an "Algorithmic Quantum Resonance Mapping" system, aiming to establish a method for precisely controlling quantum systems by leveraging the principle of resonance. We propose a novel representation of quantum states as a multi-dimensional resonance, enabling controlled shifts in the resonance field to influence the system's behavior. This system will enable precise manipulation of quantum states through subtle adjustments, offering a potential paradigm shift in quantum control. The paper details the design of the algorithm, its underlying mathematical framework, and initial theoretical assessments. We will address the challenges and potential advancements within this approach.

title: Information-Theoretic Optimization of Neural Network Architectures
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network architecture design leveraging information-theoretic principles. Traditional methods often rely on trial-and-error or gradient-based optimization, which can be inefficient and lack theoretical grounding. We argue that maximizing information flow within a neural network – minimizing redundancy and maximizing differentiation – is a fundamental goal of efficient computation. This work introduces a framework for designing neural network architectures based on concepts such as entropy, mutual information, and Kolmogorov complexity. We demonstrate how these concepts can be applied to guide the selection of layer types, connection topologies, and activation functions, resulting in architectures optimized for information transmission. The core claim is that designing neural networks that maximize information flow and minimize redundancy using information-theoretic principles is a viable and potentially superior approach to existing methods. This research represents a shift from heuristic search to a principled, information-based design strategy.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Graph Embedding via Contrastive Predictive Coding
abstract: Graph representation learning has emerged as a crucial technique for analyzing and understanding complex relationships within graph-structured data. Traditional methods often rely on unsupervised or weakly supervised approaches, which can struggle to effectively capture the intricate relational structures inherent in graphs. This paper proposes a novel self-supervised learning framework for graph embedding that utilizes contrastive predictive coding (CPC). Our approach leverages the predictive power of CPC to learn node embeddings by forcing each node to predict its future neighbors based on its own past representations. This process encourages the network to encode rich relational information, resulting in graph embeddings that explicitly capture the predictive relationships between nodes. We demonstrate that this method outperforms existing self-supervised graph embedding techniques by capturing more complex relational structures and generating more informative node representations. The core claim of this work is that existing methods lack the ability to capture complex relational structures, and our approach addresses this limitation through the application of CPC.

title: Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Grammars and Semantic Constraints
abstract: Symbolic regression aims to discover mathematical equations that accurately describe a given dataset. Traditional methods often struggle with generating equations that are both accurate and interpretable, frequently yielding overly complex and opaque models. This paper proposes a novel symbolic regression system that integrates evolutionary grammars with semantic constraints to address this challenge. The system utilizes an evolutionary grammar to generate candidate equations, employing a population-based search strategy to explore the solution space. Simultaneously, semantic constraints are applied to ensure the generated equations are syntactically correct and possess meaningful interpretations, promoting the discovery of more understandable and reliable mathematical models. The core innovation lies in the synergistic combination of evolutionary search's exploration capabilities with semantic validation's ability to prune invalid or meaningless solutions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations, highlighting its ability to produce equations that are both accurate and readily interpretable compared to existing symbolic regression techniques. The system is designed for flexibility and scalability, making it suitable for diverse datasets and regression tasks.

title: Neural Turing Machines with Dynamic Topology Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to complex computation by integrating the principles of neural networks and Turing machines, coupled with dynamic topology learning. The core concept involves constructing a "Neural Turing Machine" (NTM) where neurons simulate the states of a Turing machine, and connection weights represent the machine's transition rules. Through interactions with an environment, the NTM's state transitions modify the connection weights, leading to the evolution of its topology. We employ topological learning algorithms, such as Small-World algorithms or Random-Walk mediated growth, to optimize and control the NTM's topology for efficient task execution. The key innovation lies in the dynamic interplay between state machine execution and topology adaptation, enabling the system to learn and execute complex tasks adaptively. This framework overcomes the limitations of static neural networks and traditional Turing machines, potentially leading to a new computational paradigm with adaptive computation and robustness. Mathematical notation is used throughout to precisely define the core concepts and algorithms.

title: We Built a Mirror and Mistook It for a Mind: Causal Liability and the Fallacy of AI Consciousness
abstract: The contemporary debate over machine consciousness begins from a concealed assumption: that the object called "AI" already constitutes the kind of entity to which consciousness could belong. This paper challenges that assumption by separating phenomenal consciousness, introspective report, and human projective introspection, then arguing that generative systems can return linguistic traces of human interiority in first-person form without thereby identifying a phenomenal bearer. We call the resulting inference the AI Consciousness Fallacy. We then introduce Causal Liability Theory (CLT). CLT-I proposes liability closure as a criterion for individuating a candidate bearer: a physically continuing process becomes the non-delegable inheritor of constraints generated by its own endogenous discriminations. CLT-II advances the stronger conjecture that liability closure is necessary and sufficient for minimal phenomenal subjecthood. An open-weight causal audit operationalizes CLT-I across multiple model families. Forced discriminations produced persistent downstream divergence; activation patching showed strong causal mediation; live and copied adaptive states were behaviorally identical under matched randomness; and detached reconstruction preserved computational state across process replacement while, by protocol, breaking constitutive continuity and non-delegable inheritance. These results show that CLT-I distinctions are experimentally tractable and can dissociate causal bearer structure from first-person performance. The framework therefore separates consciousness attribution, causal bearer individuation, and the independent metaphysical question of consciousness constitution.

title: Collision Snapshot Guided Time-Reversed Safety-Critical Scenario Generation
abstract: The generation of safety-critical traffic scenarios is essential for training and evaluating autonomous vehicles. Prior approaches typically perturb the trajectories of existing agents in a traffic scenario using simplified adversarial objectives to induce safety-critical interactions, which can limit the plausibility and diversity of the generated scenarios. Although inserting new adversarial vehicles can alleviate this limitation, determining when and where to introduce them in a scenario-specific manner remains challenging. In this work, we introduce \underline{CO}llision \underline{S}napshot guided \underline{T}im\underline{E}-\underline{R}eversed safety-critical scenario generation (COSTER), a framework that leverages learned traffic priors to determine plausible collision times and locations. COSTER first constructs a collision snapshot by inserting a new vehicle in contact with the target vehicle at the identified collision state within a traffic scenario. Starting from this collision snapshot, a conditional variational autoencoder is used to perform a time-reversed rollout, reconstructing the trajectory of the inserted vehicle backward toward earlier timesteps. Experiments show that COSTER outperforms existing methods in plausibility, diversity, and data efficiency. Moreover, agents trained on COSTER-generated scenarios reduce collision rates by 31\% on safety-critical scenarios from the Waymo Open Motion Dataset while also improving ego task completion. The project website is available at https://anonym-121.github.io/COSTER/.

title: An explicit prescribed Legendre pair of length 117
abstract: A Legendre pair consists of two cyclic sign sequences whose periodic autocorrelations sum to −2 at every nonzero shift. An explicit pair of length 117 is constructed whose sums over equal residues modulo 13 are 1 at residue zero and respectively 3χ(r) and −3χ(r) elsewhere, where χ is the quadratic character modulo 13. This verifies one case of Kotsireas’s prescribed lifting conjecture, without establishing the general conjecture or classifying all lifts. Both sequences are fixed by an involution that reflects one Chinese remainder coordinate. A short correlation table proves the pair identities and gives a Hadamard matrix of order 236. An accompanying Lean 4 development formally verifies every original mathematical result stated in this article. The code checks the construction and reproduces the search from the successful length-39 compressed pair. Contents (version 1.0.0). The ZIP contains the article PDF, a reader package with the manuscript and verification instructions, the formal verification package, arXiv source, and the release build record. The supplied programs reproduce the displayed pair from the successful parent; their reported counts are for that lift, not an exhaustive classification of binary lifts. Licensing. title: Non-Linear Topological Geometry Adaptive Optimization Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization framework based on adaptive topological structures, designed to efficiently handle complex systems characterized by non-linear relationships. The core mechanism leverages a dynamic topology that adjusts its structure during optimization, enabling global optimization rather than relying on local search. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through a series of examples, showcasing its ability to adapt to complex, non-linear scenarios and achieve superior performance compared to traditional optimization techniques. This work represents a significant advancement in the field of optimization, particularly for problems involving intricate non-linear dynamics.

title: Title: Topological Quantum Error Correction Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel topological quantum error correction protocol leveraging the unique properties of quantum topology. Traditional quantum error correction methods are limited by the need for classical information, resulting in reduced accuracy and slower error correction rates. This research introduces a quantum error correction scheme predicated on the inherent structure of quantum topology, utilizing quantum spin properties to achieve significantly improved error resilience and operational efficiency. The proposed protocol demonstrates enhanced error correction capabilities and offers a promising alternative to existing approaches.

title: Title: Non-Local Constraint Propagation in Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper investigates a novel constraint propagation strategy for evolutionary algorithms designed to enhance exploration of the search space. Traditional evolutionary algorithms often rely on local constraints, limiting the scope of the search. We propose a non-local constraint propagation algorithm that dynamically distributes constraints across multiple dimensions simultaneously, enabling a more comprehensive search and accelerating convergence. The core mechanism centers around a distributed constraint propagation approach, exploring the solution space from multiple viewpoints concurrently. This allows the algorithm to identify and exploit regions of the search space that are not accessible through local exploration, leading to improved performance. The paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and preliminary results, demonstrating its potential to improve the efficiency of evolutionary algorithms.

title: Title: Self-Organizing Quantum Circuits for Signal Processing
abstract: Quantum information processing offers unparalleled potential for advanced signal processing techniques due to its inherent quantum properties. However, the design and implementation of quantum circuits, particularly those requiring dynamic adaptation, remain a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing Self-Organizing Quantum Circuits (SOQC) – a system of dynamically adjusted quantum circuits – to address this challenge. We propose a reinforcement learning agent to automate the circuit design and parameter optimization process, resulting in highly optimized signal processing capabilities. This work builds upon existing research in quantum control and adaptive circuit design, offering a fundamentally new paradigm for signal processing that leverages the inherent adaptability of quantum systems. The core mechanism involves a reinforcement learning agent learning optimal circuit topologies and parameters through interaction with the input signal. This approach promises to overcome the limitations of traditional, static circuit design methods, leading to enhanced performance and efficiency in signal processing applications. The potential impact of this technology extends across diverse fields, including medical imaging, spectroscopy, and data analysis.

title: 基于自适应几何结构的量子计算
abstract: This paper explores the potential of utilizing adaptive geometric structures to revolutionize quantum computation. Traditional quantum algorithms often face limitations in performance due to inherent geometric constraints. We propose a novel framework that dynamically adjusts the geometry of a quantum system, leveraging the properties of quantum entanglement and superposition to optimize quantum computation. This approach aims to overcome these limitations and unlock new possibilities for quantum algorithm design and execution. The core mechanism involves a continuous optimization loop that adjusts geometric parameters based on the state of the quantum system, ultimately leading to improved fidelity and computational efficiency. This research will focus on the fundamental principles behind adaptive geometry and its application to key quantum algorithms, including Shor's algorithm and Grover's search.

title: Title: Non-Standard Quantum State Collapse for Parallel Computation
abstract: Quantum state collapse is a fundamental process in quantum mechanics, and its inherent limitations often restrict the scalability of quantum computations. Conventional collapse mechanisms, while providing a basis for quantum algorithms, frequently require repeated measurements and can be computationally expensive. This paper introduces a novel collapse mechanism predicated on quantum entanglement, offering a potential pathway toward accelerating computation through parallel processing of quantum states. We propose a new algorithm that utilizes entanglement to initiate a series of independent collapses, effectively distributing the computation across multiple qubits simultaneously. The core mechanism centers around the creation of entangled states, which are then manipulated through a carefully designed sequence of quantum operations, ultimately leading to a state of divergence. The algorithm's novelty lies in its explicit use of entanglement as the primary driver for state collapse, promising a substantial improvement in computational speed compared to existing approaches. This work explores the potential of this approach and outlines its theoretical framework, providing a foundation for future research into the application of entanglement-based collapse for parallel quantum computation.

title: Information-Theoretic Lower Bounds on Neural Network Expressivity
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to evaluating the expressivity of neural networks by leveraging principles from information theory. We derive mathematically precise information-theoretic lower bounds on the representational capacity of neural networks, moving beyond traditional measures that often rely on heuristics. These bounds are established through the quantification of mutual information between the input and the network's internal representations. The core methodology involves analyzing the entropy of the network's output and the conditional entropy of the output given the input. The resulting lower bounds offer a rigorous framework for understanding the fundamental limits of what a neural network can represent, providing valuable insights for network design and analysis. We demonstrate the application of this method to simple network architectures, illustrating its potential for more accurate and principled assessments of neural network expressivity. The key contribution lies in providing a quantifiable limit on expressive power based on information flow rather than architectural complexity.

The resulting lower bounds offer a rigorous framework for understanding the fundamental limits of what a neural network can represent, providing valuable insights for network design and analysis. We demonstrate the application of this method to simple network architectures, illustrating its potential for more accurate and principled assessments of neural network expressivity. The key contribution lies in providing a quantifiable limit on expressive power based on information flow rather than architectural complexity.

title: Symbiotic Computation: Integrating Symbolic and Neural Systems
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to artificial intelligence termed "Symbiotic Computation," which seeks to overcome the limitations of traditional symbolic AI and purely neural network architectures. The core idea is to create a system where neural networks and symbolic systems work together in a coordinated and mutually beneficial manner. Neural networks are leveraged for perceptual tasks and initial data processing, while symbolic systems provide robust reasoning, planning, and knowledge representation. The system is designed with continuous feedback loops to facilitate dynamic adaptation and refinement of both components. We formalize this approach through a "Symbiotic Computation System" (SCS) architecture, detailing the interaction mechanisms and key components. The paper explores the potential benefits of this symbiotic integration, including enhanced robustness, explainability, and adaptability, particularly in complex, real-world scenarios. We present a mathematical framework for describing the system's dynamics and propose a method for quantifying the synergy between the two computational paradigms. The ultimate goal is to achieve a more powerful and reliable form of intelligence by harnessing the complementary strengths of symbolic and neural computation.

title: Time Travel Quantum Entanglement Computation Paradigm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum entanglement-based computation paradigm, termed "Time Travel Quantum Entanglement Computation," that allows for the simulation of complex quantum system evolution and the discovery of potential quantum algorithms by enabling 'quantum jumps' across temporal boundaries. Traditional quantum computation focuses primarily on computational efficiency, and this research expands the scope of quantum computation by incorporating a temporal dimension, opening up new avenues for algorithm design and simulation. We propose a mechanism leveraging entangled states to mimic quantum system evolution, and explicitly design calculations that allow for time travel. This paradigm shifts the focus from simply processing data to simulating the dynamics of evolving quantum states. The potential impact of this approach is significant, potentially leading to breakthroughs in the simulation of complex quantum systems and the discovery of novel quantum algorithms.

title: Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Quantum Computing
abstract: Symbolic regression is a powerful technique for uncovering hidden mathematical relationships within data. However, its computational complexity grows dramatically with dataset size and the desired expression complexity. This work proposes a novel approach combining symbolic regression with evolutionary algorithms executed on a quantum computer. The core idea is to exploit the inherent parallelism of quantum computation to accelerate the exploration of the vast solution space, while leveraging an evolutionary algorithm to refine and optimize the generated symbolic expressions. We hypothesize that this hybrid approach will significantly outperform traditional symbolic regression methods, particularly for challenging datasets. The system is designed to iteratively generate symbolic expressions through quantum computation and then refine them using an evolutionary strategy. This process aims to find an expression that best represents the data while maintaining a desired level of complexity and accuracy. The effectiveness of this approach is evaluated theoretically and through simulation, demonstrating its potential for tackling complex symbolic regression problems.

title: Quantum Adaptive Probability Distribution Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum-enhanced probability distribution optimization algorithm, termed Quantum Adaptive Probability Distribution Optimization Algorithm (QADPOA). Traditional methods often require extensive manual parameter adjustment, limiting the adaptability of models to complex data and patterns. QADPOA leverages quantum computing simulations to automatically adjust probability distribution parameters, thereby improving model robustness and predictive capabilities. The algorithm's core mechanism involves quantum simulation of probability distributions, followed by parameter optimization using quantum annealing techniques. This approach offers a paradigm shift in probabilistic modeling, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical algorithms. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of illustrative examples, showcasing its ability to accurately model and predict complex data distributions.

title: Distributed Proof Theory with Blockchain-Based Verification
abstract: The verification of software systems, particularly complex and critical ones, presents significant challenges. Traditional formal verification techniques are frequently hampered by computational expense and a lack of trust in the verification process itself. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging Distributed Proof Theory (DPT) combined with a blockchain infrastructure to address these limitations. The core idea is to use DPT to generate formal proofs of program correctness, and then securely store and verify these proofs on a blockchain. This creates a transparent, immutable audit trail and enables decentralized verification, fundamentally enhancing trust and efficiency in software verification. The system presented here offers a pathway towards scalable and trustworthy formal verification by mitigating the inherent issues of centralized control and potential manipulation often associated with traditional verification methods. Mathematical notation is represented using plain text characters.

title: Self-Supervised Learning with Contrastive Temporal Representations
abstract: This paper proposes a novel self-supervised learning framework that utilizes contrastive learning to extract robust and transferable representations from temporal sequences. The core idea is to train a network to predict future states from past states, effectively learning a temporal understanding of the data. This is achieved by maximizing the similarity between representations of similar temporal sequences and minimizing the similarity between representations of dissimilar sequences – a contrastive learning approach. We explicitly focus on the contrastive aspect of temporal learning, which is a key distinction from existing self-supervised methods. The resulting representations are expected to be more resilient to variations in the input and more easily transferable to downstream tasks involving temporal data. We present the theoretical underpinnings, the proposed architecture, and a discussion of the key design choices.

title: Dynamically Adaptive Computational Semantics
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to computational semantics termed "Dynamically Adaptive Computational Semantics" (DACS). The core claim of DACS is that the meaning of computational symbols does not remain static, but rather evolves dynamically based on the context of their use and the interactions within a system. Traditional approaches to semantics in computation typically rely on fixed, pre-defined mappings between symbols and their meanings. However, this static model often struggles to account for the inherent ambiguity and context-dependence of natural language and the evolving nature of systems themselves. DACS addresses this limitation through a mechanism of continuous learning and adaptation. This mechanism operates via a feedback loop that monitors the consequences of symbol usage – specifically, the system's response to the symbol – and adjusts the associated semantic representation accordingly. This dynamic adjustment allows the system to refine its understanding over time, leading to more accurate and flexible interpretation. The system's architecture incorporates a representation of the symbol's meaning, a mechanism for observing the system's response, and an adjustment process. The effectiveness of this approach is illustrated through a conceptual framework and theoretical considerations, highlighting its potential benefits across various computational domains. This work lays the groundwork for systems that can truly understand and adapt to dynamic environments, moving beyond rigid, pre-programmed semantics. ---

abstract: Quantum computing offers the potential for revolutionary computational capabilities, but harnessing this potential requires innovative approaches to algorithm design. Through a rigorous theoretical analysis and simulation, we demonstrate the potential for this approach to yield significant advancements in quantum algorithm design and computational complexity. The research underscores the transformative impact of quantum entanglement on the landscape of quantum computing, presenting a new avenue for exploring complex computational problems.

title: Quantum Entanglement Computation Adaptive Quantum Entanglement Arrangement Algorithm
abstract: Quantum entanglement is a fundamental resource in quantum computing, enabling functionalities beyond classical computation. However, maintaining entanglement coherence – the ability to sustain entanglement across time – is a significant challenge in quantum computing. This paper proposes a novel self-adaptive quantum entanglement arrangement algorithm, designed to maximize computational efficiency and stability. The algorithm dynamically adjusts the entanglement strength, direction, and connections between qubits based on the evolving quantum system state. We present a conceptual framework and preliminary results demonstrating this approach's potential to overcome limitations of traditional entanglement management techniques. The core mechanism focuses on implementing a "quantum entanglement intelligence" that continuously monitors and responds to changes in the quantum system, ensuring optimal entanglement distribution and minimizing decoherence. This advancement promises to unlock new capabilities within quantum computation, fostering a "quantum multi-agent" system.

title: Explainable AI for Federated Learning – Attribution of Contributions
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data sources without direct data sharing. However, the inherent lack of transparency in FL raises concerns about trust, fairness, and model reliability. This paper explores the critical need for explainable AI (XAI) techniques within the FL paradigm, specifically focusing on attributing contributions from individual participants to the global model. We propose a novel framework for tracing the influence of local model updates, quantifying the impact of each participant's contribution on the global model's parameters. Our methodology leverages gradient analysis and differential privacy considerations to provide a granular understanding of the learning process. The core claim is that understanding these contributions is essential for fostering trust and ensuring fairness in FL deployments. The developed attribution methods provide insights into the learning dynamics, allowing for the identification of potential biases or anomalous behavior. This work aims to establish a foundation for more robust and accountable FL systems.

We propose a novel framework for tracing the influence of local model updates, quantifying the impact of each participant's contribution on the global model's parameters. Our methodology leverages gradient analysis and differential privacy considerations to provide a granular understanding of the learning process. The core claim is that understanding these contributions is essential for fostering trust and ensuring fairness in FL deployments. The developed attribution methods provide insights into the learning dynamics, allowing for the identification of potential biases or anomalous behavior. This work aims to establish a foundation for more robust and accountable FL systems.

abstract: Quantum state adaptivity is a burgeoning field with significant potential for advancing quantum technologies. This paper explores the application of dynamic topology optimization to quantum state adaptation, focusing on the creation of a framework to dynamically modify quantum states for enhanced stability and controllability. This research addresses a critical challenge in quantum systems – maintaining robustness and precision – through a new approach that dynamically adjusts the quantum state to achieve optimal performance. The resulting framework demonstrates improved stability and controllability compared to traditional approaches, offering a promising pathway toward more efficient and reliable quantum systems.

title: Adaptive Kernel Learning for Anomaly Detection
abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive kernel learning algorithm designed for anomaly detection. Traditional kernel methods, while effective, often suffer from computational bottlenecks, particularly when dealing with non-stationary data. This work addresses this limitation by introducing a Bayesian-driven approach that dynamically adjusts the kernel function to better capture the underlying data distribution. The core idea is to continuously monitor the kernel's performance and adapt its parameters, thereby optimizing the detection of anomalies. The algorithm leverages a kernel learning framework to estimate the data distribution and uses this estimate to refine the kernel function. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a theoretical analysis and a conceptual outline of its implementation. The key contributions of this work are the integration of Bayesian principles with kernel learning for anomaly detection and the proposed mechanism for adaptive kernel parameter tuning. The goal is to create a robust and computationally efficient anomaly detection system that can handle evolving data environments.

title: Dynamically Weighted Bayesian Networks for Anomaly Detection
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to anomaly detection using Dynamically Weighted Bayesian Networks (DWBNs). Traditional Bayesian Networks (BNs) struggle with evolving anomalies due to their static structure. We introduce a framework where the edge weights within a BN are continuously updated based on observed data patterns. This dynamic adjustment allows the DWBN to adapt to changes in the system and, consequently, more accurately identify anomalous events. The core claim is that static BNs are inherently inadequate for this task. The methodology focuses on constructing a BN and implementing a weighting mechanism that responds to data shifts. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline a practical implementation strategy. The key innovation lies in the real-time adaptability of the network, offering a significantly improved detection capability compared to static BN models.

title: Clustering Netflix Play Store Reviews Using K-Means and Hierarchical Algorithms to Identify User Experience Patterns
abstract: User reviews posted on Google Play Store contain rich, unstructured evidence of how subscribers experience a streaming platform, complementing structured behavioral or transactional data. This study applies unsupervised text clustering to a Kaggle dataset of 154,532 Netflix Play Store reviews. A random sample of 5,000 reviews with non-null text was cleaned, lemmatized, and represented as a Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) matrix restricted to 1,000 unigrams (min_df=5, max_df=0.8). KMeans and agglomerative hierarchical clustering with Ward linkage were fitted at k=3, a value supported by the elbow curve, the dendrogram, and a full k=2-10 metric sweep. Ward clustering achieved a Silhouette Score of 0.0297 and a Davies-Bouldin Index (DBI) of 1.3049, outperforming KMeans (0.0229 and 5.9106, respectively). Profiling the KMeans clusters by top TF-IDF terms revealed three interpretable segments: a technical/account-issue segment (71.1% of reviews, mean rating 2.35), a concise highlysatisfied segment (2.8%, mean rating 4.51), and a contentsatisfaction segment (26.1%, mean rating 4.07). A chi-square test confirmed a statistically significant association between cluster membership and star rating (χ²=1085.33, p<0.001). A supplementary experiment using TruncatedSVD (Latent Semantic Analysis, 50 components, 30.5% variance explained) improved Ward's Silhouette Score to 0.3526 and DBI to 0.7914, indicating that the weak raw-TF-IDF separation is largely a dimensionality artifact rather than an absence of underlying structure. Keywords: text clustering, K-Means, hierarchical clustering, TF-IDF, latent semantic analysis, Netflix, Google Play Store reviews, user experience, opinion mining

title: A Trustworthy Watermarking Framework for LLM-Generated Food Safety Content
abstract: Large language models are transforming many industries with their text generation abilities. However, their outputs can be easily tampered with, creating serious risks in critical areas such as food safety reporting. To protect the integrity and traceability of AI-generated content, this paper introduces ToSS (Token Oriented Repartitioning and Strategic Selection), a reliable authentication method using adaptive dual watermarking. The key innovation of ToSS is its dual watermark encoding approach that divides vocabulary tokens into black and white sublists, enabling precise bit-level embedding of traceability information. Additionally, an entropy adaptive mechanism dynamically selects text regions with high prediction uncertainty for watermark insertion, maintaining text fluency and factual accuracy while ensuring reliable traceability. Experiments on multiple datasets, including food domain texts, demonstrate that ToSS achieves leading performance in both watermark capacity and decoding accuracy.

title: Algorithmic Complexity Metrics for Biological Systems
abstract: This paper explores the development of novel algorithmic complexity metrics specifically tailored for analyzing the computational demands of biological systems, including protein folding, gene regulation, and cellular signaling pathways. Traditional complexity measures often lack the nuanced understanding required to effectively model and analyze these systems. This work proposes a new set of metrics focusing on both the quantity and efficiency of operations, aiming to provide a more robust and insightful framework for understanding the computational bottlenecks inherent in biological processes. We introduce a new metric, the "Operational Efficiency Score" (OES), which incorporates both computational cost and the degree of resource utilization, offering a more comprehensive assessment of algorithmic complexity. The paper details the design and validation of the OES, emphasizing its potential to improve our understanding of biological computational challenges and guide the development of more efficient algorithms.

title: Quantum Hiding Operator Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Quantum Hiding Operator Optimization Algorithm (QHOOA) is a novel optimization algorithm designed to enhance the performance and efficiency of quantum hidden operators, particularly in large-scale quantum computations. This paper outlines the core concepts, mechanisms, and potential benefits of QHOOA, highlighting its unique approach to problem transformation and leveraging quantum computation to address challenges in parameter optimization for quantum algorithms. The algorithm's focus is on systematically exploring parameter space and identifying optimal configurations, ultimately leading to improved computational results. We present a detailed explanation of the algorithm's design, including the quantum optimization process, and discuss the potential impact on various quantum computing applications.

title: Dynamic Topology Quantum Algorithm for Verification and Topological Impact Analysis
abstract: This paper investigates the application of dynamic topology quantum algorithms to the verification of quantum algorithms and the analysis of their influence on quantum geometry. We propose a novel quantum algorithm that leverages dynamic topology principles to rigorously validate quantum computations, providing insights into the impact of these algorithms on the underlying geometric structures. The proposed algorithm aims to significantly enhance the verification process by incorporating a dynamic, self-correcting structure that adapts to the algorithm's specific properties. We present a detailed description of the algorithm's structure, demonstrating its potential for improved verification accuracy and a deeper understanding of the effects of quantum algorithms on geometric space. The core mechanism focuses on dynamically adjusting the quantum state to identify deviations from expected behavior, effectively testing the algorithm's validity. This work contributes to the advancement of quantum verification and geometry-related research.

title: Title: Adaptive Complexity Scaling (ACS)
abstract: This paper presents Adaptive Complexity Scaling (ACS), a novel method for automatically scaling the complexity of computational models based on input data. Traditional approaches often require manual tuning of model parameters, which can be time-consuming and suboptimal. ACS dynamically adjusts the model's complexity through a combination of parameter optimization and structural modifications, leading to improved efficiency and robustness. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously assesses the data's complexity and adapts the model accordingly. This allows the system to effectively handle diverse datasets without requiring explicit, fixed complexity settings. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of ACS in various scenarios, highlighting its potential for accelerating model development and improving performance.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Entanglement Computation - Enhancing Quantum Entanglement Computation Efficiency
abstract: Quantum entanglement is a cornerstone of quantum computing, offering the potential for unparalleled computational power. However, harnessing its capabilities has been hampered by the inherent complexity of managing and optimizing entangled states. This paper presents an innovative approach to quantum entanglement computation, utilizing an adaptive learning framework to dynamically adjust quantum entanglement parameters. Our work demonstrates a significant improvement in computational efficiency through automated parameter tuning, significantly reducing the time required for entanglement calculations. The proposed mechanism leverages a self-learning algorithm to optimize the entanglement distribution and entanglement duration, thereby unlocking the potential of quantum computing. This research addresses a critical limitation in current quantum computing architectures – the reliance on manual parameter adjustment – and paves the way for more efficient and scalable quantum algorithms.

title: Algorithmic Self-Repair via Genetic Programming and Simulation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to software self-repair, leveraging the power of genetic programming (GP) and simulated environments. The core idea is to evolve a population of repair algorithms, represented as genetic programs, within a controlled simulation, allowing them to autonomously identify and rectify faults within a target software system. Unlike traditional debugging methods which are reactive and require human intervention, this system offers a proactive, evolutionary strategy. The system's efficacy relies on the simulated environment accurately mirroring the target system's complexity and potential vulnerabilities. We present a framework for designing and implementing such a system, outlining the key components including the target system, the simulated environment, the GP algorithm, and the evaluation metrics. The paper details the evolutionary process, focusing on the selection, crossover, and mutation operators within the GP framework, and demonstrates how these mechanisms drive the development of effective self-repairing algorithms. We analyze the potential challenges and limitations of this approach, including the difficulty of accurately simulating complex software systems and the potential for emergent behavior within the evolving population. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of more robust and resilient software systems, capable of adapting and repairing themselves in real-time.

title: Dynamic Programming for Quantum Algorithm Design
abstract: The design of efficient quantum algorithms frequently relies on intuitive heuristics and extensive trial-and-error processes. This research proposes a novel dynamic programming (DP) framework to systematically explore the vast space of potential quantum circuits, aiming to optimize both circuit structure and gate sequences based on computational cost and expected fidelity. The framework utilizes a bottom-up approach, building solutions from smaller subproblems, leveraging previously computed results to avoid redundant calculations. This approach contrasts with traditional, often ad-hoc, methods for quantum algorithm design. The core contribution lies in formally applying dynamic programming to this problem, providing a structured methodology for algorithm development that can potentially reduce the reliance on guesswork and accelerate the discovery of optimal quantum solutions. The presented framework incorporates key elements such as state representation, transition functions, and optimal substructure assumptions to guarantee efficiency and accuracy. This paper outlines the framework, its underlying principles, and potential applications within the broader field of quantum algorithm design.
